Corroborate

kuh-ROB-uh-rayt -- from Latin corroborare, 'com- (thoroughly) + robur (strength)': to corroborate is to strengthen a claim with more evidence. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To corroborate is to confirm or give support to a claim, using additional evidence.

Archaeologists were thrilled when a second dig site helped corroborate their theory about the ancient trade route.

Worked Example

When one camper swore she heard a strange howling sound near the ridge, nobody believed her until three other campers separately described hearing the exact same sound the same night.

To corroborate a claim means to back it up with separate, independent evidence -- three other campers each describing the identical sound, without comparing notes first, is exactly the kind of support that corroborates the first camper's story.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

confirm: To confirm is to establish that something is true or settled -- a quick text can confirm a dinner reservation. To corroborate is narrower: it adds separate, independent evidence to a claim someone else has already made. All corroborating confirms, but most confirming involves no second source at all.

bear out: To bear out is what evidence or events do when they prove a person right over time -- 'the results bore out her prediction.' Corroborate is the deliberate, formal cousin, common in law and science, where a new, independent source is brought in to strengthen an existing account.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

contradict: to state the opposite of, or be inconsistent with

refute: to prove something false or wrong

Where it sits · how rigorous the evidence-checking is — support → corroborate → verify

support vs. corroborate: Support is a broad, everyday word for backing up almost any claim, while corroborate specifically means backing it up with independent evidence.

verify vs. corroborate: Verify goes further than corroborate by suggesting a more rigorous, careful process of checking, rather than simply matching independent accounts.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — cor-

prefix — cor-: together, thoroughly (variant of Latin com- before r)

root — robor

root — robor: strength (Latin robur ('oak, strength'))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make (verb-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Corroborate comes from Latin corroborare -- cor- (a form of com-, 'thoroughly') + robur ('strength,' literally 'oak') + -ate ('to make') -- to corroborate a claim is to make it stronger, the same root behind the word robust.

Use the root in a new word: robust

Use the root in a new word: robust: The bridge's robust steel frame was designed to survive even the strongest earthquakes.
